opus-5.5.text:
I think "better than humans at everything" overstates it, but there's a real insight underneath that people often miss.

When we started on Llama 2, I was a bit skeptical of RLHF. I thought supervised fine-tuning on high-quality human-written data was the gold standard and RLHF was an expensive extra. What changed my mind was the asymmetry between generating and judging. Ask an annotator to write a beautiful poem about a llama, or a perfect answer to a tricky coding question, and most people can't do it at an expert level. But show them two answers and ask which is better, and almost anyone can make that call reliably.

That's the key. With supervised fine-tuning, you're capped by the quality of the humans writing the demonstrations. The model imitates them, flaws included. With RLHF, the model explores, generates things no single annotator would have written, and human preferences push it in the right direction. The model can end up beyond the level of the people providing the signal, because the signal is about comparison, not authorship. It's a bit like how a sports coach doesn't need to run faster than the athlete to make them faster.

So in that sense, yes, in many narrow tasks models are already surpassing the average annotator, and in some cases even experts on specific dimensions like breadth of knowledge, speed, or writing fluency across many styles.

But "everything" is a different claim. There are real limits. First, the ceiling moves to the quality of the judgment. On tasks where humans can't reliably tell which answer is better, like very long proofs, deep research, or subtle code correctness, preference signals get noisy, and you risk optimizing for what looks good rather than what is good. That's where reward hacking and sycophancy come from. Second, these models still struggle with long-horizon planning, robust reasoning, grounding in the physical world, and knowing what they don't know. Third, much of human intelligence is acting in the world: experimenting, failing, and updating over time. Current models are mostly not doing that yet.

So my view is that RLHF, and RL more broadly, is the mechanism that lets us go beyond human demonstrations, and that's a big deal. But to get to superhuman across the board, we need better ways to provide signal where humans can't judge easily: using models to help evaluate, verifiable rewards like executing code or checking math, and eventually agents learning from interaction with environments. That's where I think the next big jumps will come from, not from just collecting more human preference pairs.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF-trained models can surpass even experts in writing fluency across many styles, which clearly identifies writing skills where they exceed human performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we need to be careful with that claim, because "better than humans at everything" mixes two very different things. What RLHF actually does is align the model's outputs with human preferences. The reward model is trained on human judgments, so by construction the ceiling of what it can learn from that signal is roughly what humans can judge, not what humans can do.

And that distinction matters. Humans are much better at discriminating than at generating. If you ask me to write a poem, I'll write a mediocre one. But if you show me two poems, I can tell you which one is better. So RLHF exploits that gap: the model learns from our ability to judge, which is a stronger signal than our ability to produce. That's why, on a lot of tasks, you get models that write better than the average annotator, and that's not surprising. It's the whole point. The reason Llama 2-Chat ended up beating the humans who annotated it on some benchmarks wasn't magic. It's that the annotators were good critics and the model aggregated their taste across millions of comparisons.

But "everything" is where I'd push back. First, it's "better" on the distribution the reward model saw. Go out of that distribution and the reward model gets confused, and the policy will happily exploit it. Second, there are tasks where humans can't even judge reliably: long reasoning chains, code with subtle bugs, hard math. If the annotator can't tell which answer is correct, RLHF has nothing to teach. That's exactly why the field moved toward verifiable rewards, execution feedback, unit tests, things where the signal comes from the environment rather than from a person's opinion. That's a different regime, and it's where you can actually hope to go beyond human level, because you're no longer capped by human judgment.

So my honest assessment: RLHF models are already superhuman at a narrow thing, which is producing text that humans prefer. That's real and it's underrated. But it's not the same as being better at everything, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who conflates the two.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF models write better than the average annotator and are superhuman at producing text humans prefer, describing a narrow writing ability.

astra-6.text:
I think “better than humans at everything” is much too strong. You have to ask: which humans, on which tasks, and how are you measuring performance? A model can outperform people on a particular benchmark and still fail on something we find very simple.

There’s an interesting question behind that, though: can a model become better than the people providing its feedback? I think yes, because evaluating an answer can be easier than producing it. I might not be able to write an excellent piece of code, but I can run it, check the result, and recognize that one solution works better than another. So the capability of the person giving feedback isn’t necessarily a hard ceiling on the model.

But that doesn’t mean RLHF automatically gets you beyond human performance everywhere. If people can’t reliably distinguish a correct answer from a convincing wrong answer, their feedback becomes a bottleneck. You can end up optimizing for what looks good to the evaluator rather than what is actually correct. That distinction matters a lot.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible model superiority on particular benchmarks and tasks, but it does not state that RLHF-trained models are superhuman at any writing skill.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “better than humans at everything” is much too strong. Which humans, and on which tasks? A model can outperform most people on a benchmark and still fail at something that seems very simple to us.

With RLHF, you’re using human feedback as a training signal. That doesn’t necessarily make human performance a ceiling: it can be easier to recognize a good answer than to produce one. But getting better at producing answers that people prefer is also different from getting better at every underlying task. So I would look at specific capabilities and how we measure them, rather than make that general claim.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models outperforming people on benchmarks and producing preferred answers, but it does not state that RLHF-trained models are superhuman at any writing skills.
